title: USDA Publishes Annual Dairy Import-Licensing Notices for the 2027 Quota Year
summary: USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service published two routine Federal Register notices on Sept. 2 governing the Dairy Tariff-Rate Quota (TRQ) import licensing program: one sets the 2027 license fee at $325 per license (total program cost estimated at $631,516 across roughly 1,950 licenses), and the other shifts specified quota amounts for certain dairy articles from the historical license category to the lottery (nonhistorical) category for the 2027 quota year.
why_it_matters: These are routine annual administrative filings, not a policy change, but they set the mechanics — fees and license-category allocations — for who can import quota-limited dairy ingredients in 2027. Worth a line in the trade-policy file given the active, high-profile US-Canada dairy tariff dispute already on the company's radar.
recommended_action: No action needed; file for reference alongside the broader US-Canada tariff tracking.

title: Survey Finds Rising Recall Volume Is Eroding Consumer Trust and Buying Behavior
summary: A consumer survey commissioned by GS1 US found FDA posted 26 food recall notices in August 2026 alone, and that 67% of consumers now say they've avoided an entire food category after just one recall notice, up from 60% a year earlier; 94% say they are concerned about how often food is recalled, and the share who believe the recall system effectively protects public health fell to 80% from 85%. GS1 US published the findings via a Sept. 2 press release, with same-day coverage from Fortune and Food Safety Magazine.
why_it_matters: Dairy products have accounted for a significant share of 2026's recall notices (cottage cheese, soft cheese tied to a multiyear Listeria outbreak, ice cream), so this data quantifies a real category-avoidance risk tied to recall volume and reinforces the case for clear, fast recall communications and proactive trust-building messaging.
recommended_action: Share the survey findings with communications and consumer-insights teams; use as supporting data when reviewing the recall-response and consumer-trust messaging playbook.

title: California Legislature Passes First-of-Its-Kind 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' Food Label Bill
summary: California's Assembly Bill 2244 cleared the Legislature on Aug. 31 with unanimous votes (32-0 in the Senate, 72-0 in the Assembly) and was sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 1. The bill creates a voluntary state certification seal, "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified," for products meeting standards that exclude synthetic dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners and certain processing aids; Newsom has until Sept. 30, 2026 to sign or veto it and is reportedly expected to sign.
why_it_matters: This would be the first state-level certification program built around a UPF definition, giving California a template other states may copy; because the qualifying criteria touch additives, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners and processing aids common in flavored milk, cultured dairy and processed cheese, it creates both a potential marketing opportunity for compliant products and a competitive/labeling distinction for products that would not qualify.
recommended_action: Brief labeling/regulatory affairs on AB 2244 ahead of the Sept. 30 gubernatorial deadline; assess which products in the portfolio could qualify for the voluntary seal and which would be excluded under its additive criteria.

title: CDC/FDA Close Second Infant-Formula Botulism Outbreak, Trace It to Same Dairy Supplier as Prior Outbreak
summary: CDC and FDA formally closed the investigation into a multistate infant botulism outbreak linked to Nara Organics powdered infant formula (four infants hospitalized in California, Pennsylvania and Washington, onset April-May 2026, no deaths) after whole-genome sequencing and supply-chain records traced the contamination to the same two suppliers implicated in the 2025 ByHeart infant formula botulism outbreak, which hospitalized 48 infants in 19 states: Organic West Milk (raw organic milk) and Dairy Farmers of America (spray-drying). FDA also noted that Organic West Milk had earlier given the agency an incomplete customer list during the ByHeart investigation that omitted Nara Organics.
why_it_matters: This is the second national infant-health outbreak traced to the same organic whole-milk supply chain within about a year, and FDA's finding that a supplier withheld a customer name during an active federal investigation raises the likelihood of tighter agency scrutiny of organic dairy ingredient sourcing, spray-drying practices and supplier traceability industry-wide. No product or facility of the company is implicated, but any manufacturer sourcing organic milk powder, or working with the same cooperative network, should expect closer buyer due-diligence and possible new FDA traceability expectations for dairy ingredient suppliers.
recommended_action: Brief supply-chain/quality leadership on the Organic West Milk-Dairy Farmers of America link; confirm no shared sourcing exposure and monitor for any FDA follow-up guidance on organic dairy ingredient traceability.
date_evidence: CDC outbreak investigation page marks closure Aug. 27, 2026, corroborated by Food Safety News reporting

title: Chobani to Invest $1.2B in Pennsylvania Plant, Buying Back Keurig Dr Pepper's Equity Stake
summary: Chobani will invest approximately $1.2 billion to acquire and expand a former Keurig Dr Pepper manufacturing plant in Allentown, Pennsylvania, adding more than 900 jobs and building a 1.5-million-square-foot campus expected to source over 3 billion pounds of Pennsylvania milk annually at full capacity. As part of the transaction, Chobani is buying back Keurig Dr Pepper's roughly $800 million equity stake in the company and separately paying $125 million for the plant itself, as KDP works to reduce debt; the Allentown project is part of a more than $4 billion buildout of Chobani's U.S. manufacturing network.
why_it_matters: A major new capacity buildout by a leading yogurt/dairy processor signals rising competition for Northeast milk supply and expanding scale in the category; it carries no direct regulatory or reputational exposure for the company but is worth tracking for regional milk-sourcing and pricing dynamics and shifting competitive positioning.
recommended_action: Track regional milk-sourcing and capacity dynamics in the Northeast; no direct action needed now.

title: House Subcommittee Advances Bipartisan Bills to Federalize Packaging 'Recyclable' and 'Recycled Content' Claims
summary: On Sept. 1, 2026, the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Commerce, Manufacturing and Trade Subcommittee voice-voted to advance the PACK Act (H.R. 6832) and the Recycled Materials Attribution Act (H.R. 7502) to the full committee. The bills would set federal, third-party-certified standards for "recyclable," "compostable," "reusable" and "recycled content" packaging claims and would preempt the current patchwork of state rules; RMAA would also formally recognize mass-balance accounting for recycled-content claims.
why_it_matters: A single federal packaging-claims standard would ease compliance for a national dairy manufacturer navigating inconsistent state EPR and labeling laws (CA, CO, ME, MD, MN, OR, WA), but the mass-balance provision is already drawing greenwashing criticism from environmental advocates -- any packaging using recycled-content claims should be ready for scrutiny if the bills advance further.
recommended_action: Monitor Only; revisit if the bills clear full committee markup or draw greenwashing criticism naming specific brands or packaging claims.
